message.content:
**Freezing point of water at 10 kPa**

| Pressure | Freezing point (°C) |
|----------|---------------------|
| 10 kPa (≈ 0.1 atm) | **≈ –2.2 °C** |

---

### Why it’s lower than 0 °C

Water’s phase diagram shows that the melting/freezing point of ice decreases as the external pressure is lowered. At 1 atm (101.3 kPa) the melting point is 0 °C. When the pressure is reduced to about 0.1 atm (10 kPa), the equilibrium temperature between ice and liquid water drops to roughly –2.2 °C.

This shift is governed by the Clausius–Clapeyron relation, which describes how the slope of the phase boundary depends on the latent heat of fusion and the volume change upon melting. Because ice has a slightly larger molar volume than liquid water, lowering the pressure favors the solid phase at a lower temperature.

---

### Quick reference

- **1 atm (101.3 kPa)** → 0 °C  
- **0.1 atm (10.13 kPa)** → ≈ –2.2 °C  
- **0.01 atm (1.013 kPa)** → ≈ –5.5 °C  

So, at 10 kPa the freezing point of water is about **–2.2 °C**.
